Check:

  • 0
  • 0 (or legacy 1)
  • pairing approvals / allowlist entries (0 still requires 1)
  • group DMs use MPIM handling; enable 0 and, if configured, include the MPIM in 1
  • Slack Assistant DM events: verbose logs mentioning 0 usually mean Slack sent an edited Assistant-thread event without a recoverable human sender in message metadata

bash

openclaw pairing list slack

Socket mode not connecting

Validate bot + app tokens and Socket Mode enablement in Slack app settings. The App-Level Token needs 0, and the Bot User OAuth Token bot token must belong to the same Slack app/workspace as the app token.

If 0 shows 1 or 2, the Slack account is configured but the current runtime could not resolve the SecretRef-backed value.

Logs such as 0 are recoverable start failures. Missing scopes, revoked tokens, and invalid auth fail fast instead. A 1 log means the bot token and app token appear to belong to different Slack apps; fix the Slack app credentials.

HTTP mode not receiving events

Validate:

  • signing secret
  • webhook path
  • Slack Request URLs (Events + Interactivity + Slash Commands)
  • unique 0 per HTTP account
  • the public URL terminates TLS and forwards requests to the Gateway path
  • the Slack app 0 path exactly matches 1 (default 2)

If 0 appears in account snapshots, the HTTP account is configured but the current runtime could not resolve the SecretRef-backed signing secret.

A repeated 0 log means two HTTP accounts are using the same 1; give each account a distinct path.

Native/slash commands not firing

Verify whether you intended:

  • native command mode (0) with matching slash commands registered in Slack
  • or single slash command mode (0)

Slack does not create or remove slash commands automatically. 0 does not enable Slack native commands; use 1 and create the matching commands in the Slack app. In HTTP mode, every Slack slash command must include the Gateway URL. In Socket Mode, command payloads arrive over the websocket and Slack ignores 2.

Also check 0, DM authorization, channel allowlists, and per-channel 1 allowlists. Slack returns ephemeral errors for blocked slash-command senders, including:

  • 0
  • 0

Attachment media reference

Slack can attach downloaded media to the agent turn when Slack file downloads succeed and size limits permit. Audio clips can be transcribed, image files can pass through the media-understanding path or directly to a vision-capable reply model, and other files remain available as downloadable file context.

Supported media types
  • Slack audio clips
  • Source: Slack file URL
  • Current behavior: Downloaded and routed through shared audio transcription
  • Notes: Requires files:read and a working tools.media.audio model or CLI
  • JPEG / PNG / GIF / WebP images
  • Source: Slack file URL
  • Current behavior: Downloaded and attached to the turn for vision-capable handling
  • Notes: Per-file cap: channels.slack.mediaMaxMb (default 20 MB)
  • PDF files
  • Source: Slack file URL
  • Current behavior: Downloaded and exposed as file context for tools such as download-file or pdf
  • Notes: Slack inbound does not convert PDFs into image-vision input automatically
  • Other files
  • Source: Slack file URL
  • Current behavior: Downloaded when possible and exposed as file context
  • Notes: Binary files are not treated as image input
  • Thread replies
  • Source: Thread starter files
  • Current behavior: Root-message files can be hydrated as context when the reply has no direct media
  • Notes: File-only starters use an attachment placeholder
  • Multi-file messages
  • Source: Multiple Slack files
  • Current behavior: Each file is evaluated independently
  • Notes: Slack processing is capped at eight files per message
Inbound pipeline

When a Slack message with file attachments arrives:

  1. OpenClaw downloads the file from Slack’s private URL using the bot token.
  2. The file is written to the media store on success.
  3. Downloaded media paths and content types are added to the inbound context.
  4. Audio clips are routed to the shared transcription pipeline; image-capable model/tool paths can use image attachments from the same context.
  5. Other files remain available as file metadata or media references for tools that can handle them.
Thread-root attachment inheritance

When a message arrives in a thread (has a 0 parent):

  • If the reply itself has no direct media and the included root message has files, Slack can hydrate the root files as thread-starter context.
  • Root files are hydrated only while seeding a new or reset thread session. Later text-only replies reuse the existing session context and do not reattach root files as fresh media.
  • Direct reply attachments take precedence over root-message attachments.
  • A root message that has only files and no text is represented with an attachment placeholder so the fallback can still include its files.
Multi-attachment handling

When a single Slack message contains multiple file attachments:

  • Each attachment is processed independently through the media pipeline.
  • Downloaded media references are aggregated into the message context.
  • Processing order follows Slack’s file order in the event payload.
  • A failure in one attachment’s download does not block others.
Size, download, and model limits
  • Size cap: Default 20 MB per file. Configurable via 0.
  • Audio transcription cap: the selected audio-capable 0 entry’s 1 also applies when the downloaded file is sent to a transcription provider or CLI.
  • Download failures: Files that Slack cannot serve, expired URLs, inaccessible files, oversize files, and Slack auth/login HTML responses are skipped instead of being reported as unsupported formats.
  • Vision model: Image analysis uses the active reply model when it supports vision, or the image model configured at 0.
Known limits
  • Expired Slack file URL
  • Current behavior: File skipped; no error shown
  • Workaround: Re-upload the file in Slack
  • Audio transcription unavailable
  • Current behavior: Clip remains attached but no transcript is produced
  • Workaround: Configure tools.media.audio or install a supported local transcription CLI
  • Captionless clip does not pass a mention gate
  • Current behavior: Dropped after private speculative transcription; transcript and download discarded
  • Workaround: Configure a spoken-name mention pattern, add a typed bot mention, or use a DM
  • Vision model not configured
  • Current behavior: Image attachments are stored as media references, but not analyzed as images
  • Workaround: Configure agents.defaults.imageModel or use a vision-capable reply model
  • Very large images (> 20 MB by default)
  • Current behavior: Skipped per size cap
  • Workaround: Increase channels.slack.mediaMaxMb if Slack allows
  • Forwarded/shared attachments
  • Current behavior: Text and Slack-hosted image/file media are best-effort
  • Workaround: Re-share directly in the OpenClaw thread
  • PDF attachments
  • Current behavior: Stored as file/media context, not automatically routed through image vision
  • Workaround: Use download-file for file metadata or the pdf tool for PDF analysis
Related documentation
  • Media understanding pipeline
  • Audio and voice notes
  • PDF tool

SMS

Get started

OpenClaw receives and sends SMS through a Twilio phone number or Messaging Service. The Gateway registers an inbound webhook route (default 0), validates Twilio request signatures by default, and sends replies back through Twilio’s Messages API.

Status: official plugin, installed separately. Text only: no MMS/media, direct messages only.

Pairing

Default DM policy for SMS is pairing.

Gateway security

Review webhook exposure and sender access controls.

Channel troubleshooting

Cross-channel diagnostics and repair playbooks.

Before you begin

You need:

  • The official SMS plugin installed with 0.
  • A Twilio account with an SMS-capable phone number, or a Twilio Messaging Service.
  • The Twilio Account SID and Auth Token.
  • A public HTTPS URL that reaches your OpenClaw Gateway.
  • A sender policy choice: 0 (default) for private use, 1 for preapproved phone numbers, or 2 only for intentionally public SMS access.

One Twilio number can serve both SMS and Voice Call if it has both capabilities. The SMS webhook and Voice webhook are configured separately in Twilio and use separate Gateway paths; this page only covers the SMS webhook.

Quick Setup

Install the plugin

bash

openclaw plugins install @openclaw/sms
Create or choose a Twilio sender

In Twilio, open Phone Numbers > Manage > Active numbers and choose an SMS-capable number. Save:

  • Account SID, for example 0
  • Auth Token
  • Sender phone number, for example 0

If you use a Messaging Service instead of a fixed sender number, save the Messaging Service SID, for example 0.

Configure the SMS channel

Save this as 0 and change the placeholders:

json5

{channels: {sms: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: "twilio-auth-token", fromNumber: "+15551234567", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms", dmPolicy: "pairing",},},}

Apply it:

bash

openclaw config patch --file ./sms.patch.json5 --dry-runopenclaw config patch --file ./sms.patch.json5
Point Twilio at the Gateway webhook

In the Twilio phone number settings, open Messaging and set A message comes in to:

text

https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms

Use HTTP 0. The default local path is 1; change 2 if you need a different route.

Expose the exact SMS webhook path

Your public URL must route the SMS path to the Gateway process (default port 0). If you use Tailscale Funnel for local testing, expose 1 explicitly:

bash

tailscale funnel --bg --set-path /webhooks/sms http://127.0.0.1:<gateway-port>/webhooks/smstailscale funnel status

Voice Call and SMS use separate webhook paths. If the same Twilio number handles both, keep both routes configured in Twilio and in your tunnel.

Start the Gateway and approve first sender

bash

openclaw gateway

Send a text message to the Twilio number. The first message creates a pairing request. Approve it:

bash

openclaw pairing list smsopenclaw pairing approve sms <CODE>

Pairing codes expire after 1 hour.

Configuration Examples

All keys live under 0 (and per account under 1):

  • enabled
  • Default: true
  • Purpose: Enable or disable the channel/account.
  • accountSid
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: Twilio Account SID ( AC… ).
  • authToken
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: Twilio Auth Token; plaintext string or SecretRef.
  • fromNumber
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: E.164 sender number.
  • messagingServiceSid
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: Messaging Service SID ( MG… ) used when no fromNumber resolves.
  • defaultTo
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: Default destination when a send flow omits an explicit target.
  • webhookPath
  • Default: /webhooks/sms
  • Purpose: Gateway HTTP path for inbound Twilio webhooks.
  • publicWebhookUrl
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: Public URL configured in Twilio; required for signature validation.
  • dangerouslyDisableSignatureValidation
  • Default: false
  • Purpose: Skip X-Twilio-Signature checks; local tunnel testing only.
  • dmPolicy
  • Default: “pairing”
  • Purpose: pairing , allowlist , open , or disabled .
  • allowFrom
  • Default: []
  • Purpose: Allowed sender numbers in E.164, or “*” with dmPolicy: “open” .
  • textChunkLimit
  • Default: 1500
  • Purpose: Maximum characters per outbound SMS chunk.
  • accounts , defaultAccount
  • Default: —
  • Purpose: Multi-account map and default account id.
Config file

Use config-file setup when you want the channel definition to travel with the Gateway config:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: "twilio-auth-token", fromNumber: "+15551234567", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms", dmPolicy: "pairing", }, },}
Environment variables

Environment variables apply to the default account only; config values take precedence over env values.

  • TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
  • Maps to: accountSid
  • TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN
  • Maps to: authToken
  • TWILIO_PHONE_NUMBER (alias TWILIO_SMS_FROM )
  • Maps to: fromNumber
  • TWILIO_MESSAGING_SERVICE_SID
  • Maps to: messagingServiceSid
  • SMS_PUBLIC_WEBHOOK_URL
  • Maps to: publicWebhookUrl
  • SMS_WEBHOOK_PATH
  • Maps to: webhookPath
  • SMS_ALLOWED_USERS
  • Maps to: allowFrom (comma-separated)
  • SMS_TEXT_CHUNK_LIMIT
  • Maps to: textChunkLimit
  • SMS_DANGEROUSLY_DISABLE_SIGNATURE_VALIDATION
  • Maps to: dangerouslyDisableSignatureValidation ( “true” )

bash

export TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID="ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"export TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN="<twilio-auth-token>"export TWILIO_PHONE_NUMBER="+15551234567"export SMS_PUBLIC_WEBHOOK_URL="https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms"

Then enable the channel in config:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { enabled: true, dmPolicy: "pairing", }, },}
SecretRef auth token

0 can be a SecretRef (1). Use this when the Gateway should resolve the Twilio Auth Token from the OpenClaw secrets runtime instead of storing plaintext config:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: { source: "env", provider: "default", id: "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN" }, fromNumber: "+15551234567", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms", dmPolicy: "pairing", }, },}

The referenced environment variable or secret provider must be visible to the Gateway runtime. Restart managed Gateway processes after changing host environment variables.

Messaging Service sender

Use 0 instead of 1 when Twilio should choose the sender through a Messaging Service:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: "twilio-auth-token", messagingServiceSid: "MGxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms", dmPolicy: "pairing", }, },}

If both 0 and 1 are present after config and env resolution, 2 is used.

Default outbound target

Set 0 when automation or agent-initiated delivery should have a default destination if a send flow omits an explicit target:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: "twilio-auth-token", fromNumber: "+15551234567", defaultTo: "+15557654321", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms", }, },}

Access control

0 controls direct SMS access:

  • 0 (default): unknown senders get a pairing code; approve with 1.
  • 0: only senders in 1 are processed. An empty 2 rejects every sender (the Gateway logs a startup warning).
  • 0: config validation requires 1 to include 2. Without the wildcard, only listed numbers can chat.
  • 0: all inbound DMs are dropped.

0 entries should be E.164 phone numbers such as 1. 2 and 3 prefixes are accepted and normalized. For a private assistant, prefer 4 with explicit phone numbers:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: "twilio-auth-token", fromNumber: "+15551234567", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms", dmPolicy: "allowlist", allowFrom: ["+15557654321"], }, },}

Sending SMS

With the SMS channel selected, targets accept bare E.164 numbers or the 0 prefix:

bash

openclaw message send --channel sms --target sms:+15551234567 --message "hello"

When channel selection is implicit, the 0 prefix selects this channel without taking over the 1 service prefix, which iMessage uses to pick carrier SMS delivery for its own targets:

bash

openclaw message send --target twilio-sms:+15551234567 --message "hello"

The CLI requires an explicit 0. 1 is for automation and agent-initiated delivery paths where the target can be resolved from channel config.

Agent replies from inbound SMS conversations automatically go back to the sender through the configured Twilio sender.

SMS output is plain text. OpenClaw strips markdown, flattens fenced code blocks, rewrites links as 0, and splits long replies into chunks of at most 1 characters (default 1500) before sending them through Twilio.

Verify Setup

After the Gateway starts:

  1. Confirm the Gateway log shows the SMS webhook route.
  2. Run a Twilio-side probe (checks the configured Twilio webhook URL/method and recent inbound errors):

bash

openclaw channels capabilities --channel smsopenclaw channels status --channel sms --probe --json
  1. Send an SMS to the Twilio number from your phone.
  2. Run 0.
  3. Approve the pairing code with 0.
  4. Send another SMS and confirm the agent replies.

For outbound-only testing, use:

bash

openclaw message send --channel sms --target sms:+15557654321 --message "OpenClaw SMS test"
End-to-end test from macOS iMessage/SMS

On a Mac that can send carrier SMS through Messages, you can use 0 to drive the sender side without touching your phone:

bash

imsg send --to "+15551234567" --service sms --text "OpenClaw SMS E2E $(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)" --jsonopenclaw pairing list smsopenclaw pairing approve sms <CODE>imsg send --to "+15551234567" --service sms --text "reply exactly SMS pong" --json

The first message should create a pairing request. The second message should receive the agent reply through Twilio.

Webhook security

By default, OpenClaw validates 0 using 1 and 2. Keep the endpoint portion of 3 byte-for-byte aligned with the URL configured in Twilio, including scheme, host, path, and query string. OpenClaw excludes Twilio connection-override fragments (4) from signature computation, as Twilio requires.

The webhook route also enforces, independent of signature validation:

  • 0 only.
  • Failed-request budget of 300 requests per minute per SMS account, webhook route, and resolved client address. All requests count toward this budget, but HTTP 429 is applied only after body parsing or Twilio signature validation fails.
  • Dispatchable callback rate limit of 30 accepted callbacks per minute per SMS account, webhook route, and validated sender after body parsing and signature validation pass (HTTP 429 above that). The sender key is the canonicalized, signature-covered 0 value, so equivalent SMS/RCS address forms share one budget, one flooding sender exhausts only its own budget, and callbacks from other senders behind Twilio’s shared egress addresses remain dispatchable. Invalid or missing sender values share a separate empty-sender budget.
  • Aggregate validated-callback ceiling of 300 accepted callbacks per minute per SMS account and webhook route. This bounds durable-ingress pressure from many distinct signed senders without recreating shared-egress cross-throttling. If signature validation is disabled, nothing authenticates 0; the stricter 30/min resolved-client-address dispatch cap applies instead of the validated sender and aggregate policy.
  • Client addresses are resolved through the shared Gateway trusted-proxy rules. If 0 contains the reverse proxy that forwards Twilio callbacks, OpenClaw keys the address-based limits from the forwarded client address; otherwise it falls back to the direct socket address.
  • The payload 0 must match the configured 1. The raw callback is first committed to the durable ingress queue and acknowledged; a mismatch is then marked as a permanent invalid-payload failure during drain and is never dispatched.
  • Replayed 0 values are deduplicated by the durable ingress queue. Completed-message tombstones are retained for 24 hours (up to 20,000 entries per account); permanent-failure tombstones are retained for 30 days (up to 1,000 entries).
  • Request bodies over 32 KB are rejected.

Twilio does not retry HTTP 429 by default. The 0 and 1 connection overrides opt into 4xx retries, but Twilio caps the complete retry transaction at 15 seconds. Configure a fallback URL when another handler must receive failed deliveries; treat a 429 as a fail-closed rejection, not reliable backpressure.

For local tunnel testing only, you can set:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { dangerouslyDisableSignatureValidation: true, }, },}

Do not use disabled signature validation on a public Gateway.

Multi-account config

Use 0 when you operate more than one Twilio number:

json5

{ channels: { sms: { accounts: { support: { enabled: true, accountSid: "ACxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", authToken: "twilio-auth-token", fromNumber: "+15551234567", publicWebhookUrl: "https://gateway.example.com/webhooks/sms/support", webhookPath: "/webhooks/sms/support", dmPolicy: "allowlist", allowFrom: ["+15557654321"], }, }, }, },}

Each account must use a distinct 0; the Gateway refuses to register a webhook route whose path is already owned by another account. 1/2 environment fallbacks apply only to the default account; set 3 to change which account that is.

Troubleshooting

Twilio returns 403 or OpenClaw rejects the webhook

Check that 0 exactly matches the URL configured in Twilio, including scheme, host, path, and query string. Twilio signs the public URL string, so proxy rewrites and alternate hostnames can break signature validation.

A 403 with 0 means the inbound payload’s 1 does not match the configured 2; check that the webhook points at the account that owns the number.

No pairing request appears

Check the Twilio number’s Messaging webhook URL and method. It must point to the SMS webhook URL and use 0. Also confirm the Gateway is reachable from the public internet or through your tunnel.

If the Twilio message log shows error 0, Twilio accepted the inbound SMS but could not reach your webhook. Check:

  • Twilio Messaging > A message comes in points at 0.
  • The method is 0.
  • The tunnel or reverse proxy exposes the exact 0; for Tailscale Funnel, run 1 and confirm 2 is listed.
  • 0 uses the same scheme, host, path, and query string Twilio sends, so signature validation can reproduce the signed URL.

0 surfaces both mismatched Twilio webhook settings and recent 1 errors.

Outbound sends fail

Confirm 0, 1, and either 2 or 3 are resolved. If you use a trial Twilio account, the destination number may need to be verified in Twilio before outbound SMS will send.

Messages arrive but the agent does not answer

Check 0 and 1. With the default 2 policy, the sender must be approved before normal agent turns are processed.

Synology Chat

ChannelsDeveloper and self-hosted

Synology Chat connects to OpenClaw through a webhook pair: a Synology Chat outgoing webhook posts inbound direct messages to the Gateway, and replies go back through a Synology Chat incoming webhook.

Status: official plugin, installed separately. Direct messages only; text and URL-based file sends are supported.

Install

bash

openclaw plugins install @openclaw/synology-chat

Local checkout (when running from a git repo):

bash

openclaw plugins install ./path/to/local/synology-chat-plugin

Details: Plugins

Quick setup

  1. Install the plugin (above).
  2. In Synology Chat integrations:
  • Create an incoming webhook and copy its URL.
  • Create an outgoing webhook with your secret token.
  1. Point the outgoing webhook URL to your OpenClaw Gateway:
  • 0 by default.
  • Or your custom 0.
  1. Finish setup in OpenClaw. Synology Chat appears in the same channel setup list in both flows:
  • Guided: 0 or 1
  • Direct: 0
  1. Restart the Gateway and send a DM to the Synology Chat bot.

Webhook auth details:

  • OpenClaw accepts the outgoing webhook token from 0, then 1, then headers.
  • Accepted header forms:
  • 0
  • 0
  • 0
  • 0
  • Empty or missing tokens fail closed.
  • Payloads may be 0 or 1; 2, 3, and 4 are required.

Inbound durability

After token, sender-policy, and rate-limit checks pass, OpenClaw removes the webhook token from the stored envelope and durably queues the event before acknowledging it. The route returns 0 only after that append succeeds; a persistence failure returns 1 so Synology Chat can retry instead of silently losing the message. The durable 2 carries 3; authentication, validation, and storage-error responses omit the marker, so reverse proxies can require it to distinguish durable acceptance from a generic response.

Pending or retryable events survive a Gateway restart. Synology’s stable 0 suppresses duplicate queue entries while the corresponding active or retained completion record exists. Delivery remains at least once across the queue-to-agent handoff, so a crash at that boundary can still replay a turn.

Minimal config:

json5

{ channels: { "synology-chat": { enabled: true, token: "synology-outgoing-token", incomingUrl: "https://nas.example.com/webapi/entry.cgi?api=SYNO.Chat.External&method=incoming&version=2&token=...", webhookPath: "/webhook/synology", dmPolicy: "allowlist", allowedUserIds: ["123456"], rateLimitPerMinute: 30, allowInsecureSsl: false, }, },}

Environment variables

For the default account, you can use env vars:

  • 0
  • 0
  • 0
  • 0 (comma-separated)
  • 0
  • 0

Config values override env vars.

0 and 1 cannot be set from a workspace 2; see Workspace 3 files.

DM policy and access control

  • Supported 0 values: 1 (default), 2, and 3. Synology Chat has no pairing flow; approve senders by adding their numeric Synology user IDs to 4.
  • 0 accepts a list (or comma-separated string) of Synology user IDs.
  • In 0 mode, an empty 1 list is treated as misconfiguration and the webhook route will not start.
  • 0 allows public DMs only when 1 includes 2; with restrictive entries, only matching users can chat. 3 with an empty 4 list also refuses to start the route.
  • 0 blocks DMs.
  • Reply recipient binding stays on stable numeric 0 by default. 1 is break-glass compatibility mode that re-enables mutable username/nickname lookup for reply delivery.

Outbound delivery

Use numeric Synology Chat user IDs as targets. The 0, 1, and 2 prefixes are accepted.

Examples:

bash

openclaw message send --channel synology-chat --target 123456 --message "Hello from OpenClaw"openclaw message send --channel synology-chat --target synology-chat:123456 --message "Hello again"openclaw message send --channel synology-chat --target synology:123456 --message "Short prefix"

Outbound text is chunked at 2000 characters. Media sends are supported by URL-based file delivery: the NAS downloads and attaches the file (max 32 MB). Outbound file URLs must use 0 or 1, and private or otherwise blocked network targets are rejected before OpenClaw forwards the URL to the NAS webhook.

Multi-account

Multiple Synology Chat accounts are supported under 0. Each account can override token, incoming URL, webhook path, DM policy, and limits. Direct-message sessions are isolated per account and user, so the same numeric 1 on two different Synology accounts does not share transcript state. Give each enabled account a distinct 2. OpenClaw rejects duplicate exact paths and refuses to start named accounts that only inherit a shared webhook path in multi-account setups. If you intentionally need legacy inheritance for a named account, set 3 on that account or at 4, but duplicate exact paths are still rejected fail-closed. Prefer explicit per-account paths.

json5

{ channels: { "synology-chat": { enabled: true, accounts: { default: { token: "token-a", incomingUrl: "https://nas-a.example.com/...token=...", }, alerts: { token: "token-b", incomingUrl: "https://nas-b.example.com/...token=...", webhookPath: "/webhook/synology-alerts", dmPolicy: "allowlist", allowedUserIds: ["987654"], }, }, }, },}

Security notes

  • Keep 0 secret and rotate it if leaked.
  • Keep 0 unless you explicitly trust a self-signed local NAS cert.
  • Inbound webhook requests are token-verified and rate-limited per sender (0, default 30).
  • Invalid token checks use constant-time secret comparison and fail closed; repeated invalid-token attempts temporarily lock out the source IP.
  • Inbound message text is sanitized against known prompt-injection patterns and truncated at 4000 characters.
  • Prefer 0 for production.
  • Keep 0 off unless you explicitly need legacy username-based reply delivery.
  • Keep 0 off unless you explicitly accept shared-path routing risk in a multi-account setup.

Troubleshooting

  • 0:
  • the outgoing webhook payload is missing one of the required fields
  • if Synology sends the token in headers, make sure the gateway/proxy preserves those headers
  • 0:
  • the outgoing webhook secret does not match 0
  • the request is hitting the wrong account/webhook path
  • a reverse proxy stripped the token header before the request reached OpenClaw
  • 0:
  • too many invalid token attempts from the same source can temporarily lock that source out
  • authenticated senders also have a separate per-user message rate limit
  • 0:
  • 0 is enabled but no users are configured
  • 0:
  • the sender’s numeric 0 is not in 1

  • Groups — group chat behavior and mention gating
  • Channel Routing — session routing for messages
  • Security — access model and hardening

Telegram

ChannelsMainstream messaging

Production-ready for bot DMs and groups via grammY. Long polling is the default transport; webhook mode is optional.

Pairing

Default DM policy for Telegram is pairing.

Channel troubleshooting

Cross-channel diagnostics and repair playbooks.

Gateway configuration

Full channel config patterns and examples.

Quick setup

Create the bot token in BotFather

Both flows end with a token you paste into OpenClaw — pick one:

  • Chat flow: open Telegram, chat with @BotFather (confirm the handle is exactly 0), run 1, follow the prompts, and save the token.
  • Web flow: open BotFather’s web app — it runs in every Telegram client, including web.telegram — create the bot in the UI, and copy its token.
Configure token and DM policy

json5

{channels: {telegram: { enabled: true, botToken: "123:abc", dmPolicy: "pairing", groups: { "*": { requireMention: true } },},},}

Env fallback: 0 (default account only; named accounts must use 1 or 2). Telegram does not use 3; set the token in config/env, then start the gateway.

Start gateway and approve first DM

bash

openclaw gatewayopenclaw pairing list telegramopenclaw pairing approve telegram <CODE>

Pairing codes expire after 1 hour.

Add the bot to a group

Add the bot to your group, then get the two IDs group access needs:

  • your Telegram user ID, for 0 / 1
  • the Telegram group chat ID, as the key under 0

Get the group chat ID from 0, a forwarded-ID bot, or Bot API 1. After the group is allowed, 2 confirms the user and group IDs.

Negative supergroup IDs starting with 0 are group chat IDs. They go under 1, not 2.

Telegram side settings

Privacy mode and group visibility

Telegram bots default to Privacy Mode, which limits which group messages they receive.

To see all group messages, either:

  • disable privacy mode via 0, or
  • make the bot a group admin.

After toggling privacy mode, remove and re-add the bot in each group so Telegram applies the change.

Group permissions

Admin status is controlled in Telegram group settings. Admin bots receive all group messages, useful for always-on group behavior.

Helpful BotFather toggles

  • 0 — allow/deny group adds
  • 0 — group visibility behavior

The same settings are available in BotFather’s web app if you prefer a UI over chat commands.

Dashboard Mini App

The Dashboard Mini App opens the full OpenClaw Control UI as a Telegram WebApp. Run 0 in a DM with the bot, then tap Open dashboard. The command is registered automatically when the Telegram plugin is active; there is no separate Mini App flag.

Requirements:

  • 0 or 1 for the published HTTPS Mini App URL.
  • Your numeric Telegram user ID must be in the selected account’s effective 0 or in 1. Wildcards and usernames do not grant Mini App owner access.
  • Use a DM. In groups, 0 replies with 1 and sends no button.
  • Docker installs: Serve/Funnel modes require the gateway to bind loopback next to 0, which bridge networking with published ports cannot satisfy. Run the gateway container with 1 and mount the host 2 socket (3) plus the 4 CLI into the container.

Configure one of the supported Tailscale publishing modes:

json5

{ gateway: { tailscale: { mode: "serve", // or "funnel" }, },}

OpenClaw automatically honors 0 when selecting the published host and 1 when building the Control UI and WebSocket URLs.

When the Mini App opens, Telegram provides signed WebApp 0. OpenClaw verifies its signature with the selected bot account’s token, rejects missing, invalid, expired, or replayed data, extracts the numeric Telegram user ID, and checks owner access again before handing off to the Control UI.

If 0 cannot resolve a published HTTPS URL, it replies with:

text

Mini App needs an HTTPS gateway URL. Set `gateway.tailscale.mode: serve` or `funnel`, then retry.

Set one of the modes shown above, make sure Tailscale is running on the gateway host, and retry the command.

The Mini App is a Tailscale-only v1 path and does not support Telegram Web iframe.

Access control and activation

Group bot identity

In groups and forum topics, an explicit mention of the configured bot handle (for example 0) addresses the selected OpenClaw agent, even when the agent persona name differs from the Telegram username. Group silence policy still applies to unrelated traffic, but the bot handle itself is never “someone else.”

DM policy

0 controls direct message access:

  • 0 (default)
  • 0 (requires at least one sender ID in 1)
  • 0 (requires 1 to include 2)
  • 0

0 with 1 lets any Telegram account that finds or guesses the bot username command the bot. Use it only for intentionally public bots with tightly restricted tools; one-owner bots should use 2 with numeric user IDs.

0 accepts numeric Telegram user IDs. 1 / 2 prefixes are accepted and normalized. In multi-account configs, a restrictive top-level 3 is a safety boundary: an account-level 4 does not make that account public unless the merged effective allowlist still contains an explicit wildcard. 5 with empty 6 blocks all DMs and is rejected by config validation. Setup asks for numeric user IDs only. If your config has 7 allowlist entries from an older setup, run 8 to resolve them to numeric IDs (best-effort; requires a Telegram bot token). If you previously relied on pairing-store allowlist files, 9 can recover entries into 10 for allowlist flows (for example when 11 has no explicit IDs yet).

For one-owner bots, prefer 0 with explicit numeric 1 IDs over depending on previous pairing approvals.

Common confusion: DM pairing approval does not mean “this sender is authorized everywhere.” Pairing grants DM access only. If no command owner exists yet, the first approved pairing also sets 0, giving owner-only commands and exec approvals an explicit operator account. Group sender authorization still comes from explicit config allowlists. To be authorized for both DMs and group commands with one identity: put your numeric Telegram user ID in 1, and for owner-only commands make sure 2 contains 3.

Finding your Telegram user ID

Safer (no third-party bot): DM your bot, run 0, read 1.

Official Bot API method:

bash

curl "https://api.telegram.org/bot<bot_token>/getUpdates"

Third-party (less private): 0 or 1.

Group policy and allowlists

Two controls apply together:

  1. Which groups are allowed (0)
  • no 0 config, 1: any group passes group-ID checks
  • no 0 config, 1 (default): all groups blocked until you add 2 entries (or 3)
  • 0 configured: acts as an allowlist (explicit IDs or 1)
  1. Which senders are allowed in groups (0)
  • 0 / 1 (default) / 2

0 filters group senders; if unset, Telegram falls back to 1 (not the pairing store — group sender auth never inherits DM pairing-store approvals, a security boundary since 2). 3 entries should be numeric Telegram user IDs (4 / 5 prefixes are normalized); non-numeric entries are ignored. Do not put group or supergroup chat IDs here — negative chat IDs belong under 6. Practical pattern for one-owner bots: set your user ID in 7, leave 8 unset, and allow the target groups under 9. If 10 is entirely missing from config, runtime defaults to fail-closed 11 unless 12 is explicitly set.

Owner-only group setup:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { enabled: true, dmPolicy: "pairing", allowFrom: ["<YOUR_TELEGRAM_USER_ID>"], groupPolicy: "allowlist", groups: { "<GROUP_CHAT_ID>": { requireMention: true, }, },},},}

Test from the group with 0. Plain group messages do not trigger the bot while 1.

Allow any member in one specific group:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { groups: { "-1001234567890": { groupPolicy: "open", requireMention: false, }, },},},}

Allow only specific users inside one specific group:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { groups: { "-1001234567890": { requireMention: true, allowFrom: ["8734062810", "745123456"], }, },},},}
Mention behavior

Group replies require mention by default. A mention can come from:

  • a native 0 mention, or
  • a mention pattern in 0 or 1

Session-level toggles (state only, not persisted): 0, 1. Use config for persistence:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { groups: { "*": { requireMention: false }, },},},}

Group history context is always on and bounded by 0. Set 1 to disable the group history window. 2 removes the retired 3 key.

Getting the group chat ID: forward a group message to 0 / 1, read 2 from 3, inspect Bot API 4, or (once the group is allowed) run 5.

Runtime behavior

  • Telegram runs inside the gateway process.
  • Routing is deterministic: Telegram inbound replies back to Telegram (the model does not pick channels).
  • Inbound messages normalize into the shared channel envelope with reply metadata, media placeholders, and persisted reply-chain context for replies the gateway has observed.
  • Group sessions are isolated by group ID. Forum topics append 0.
  • DM messages can carry 0; OpenClaw preserves it for replies. DM topic sessions split only when Telegram 1 reports 2 for the bot; otherwise DMs stay on the flat session.
  • Long polling uses the grammY runner with per-chat/per-thread sequencing. Runner sink concurrency uses 0.
  • Multi-account startup bounds concurrent 0 probes so large bot fleets do not fan out every account probe at once.
  • Each gateway process guards long polling so only one active poller can use a bot token at a time. Persistent 0 409 conflicts point to another OpenClaw gateway, script, or external poller using the same token.
  • The polling watchdog restarts after 120 seconds without completed 0 liveness.
  • Telegram Bot API has no read-receipt support (0 does not apply).

Feature reference

Live stream preview (message edits)

OpenClaw streams partial replies in real time in direct chats, groups, and topics: send a preview message, then 0 repeatedly, finalizing in place.

  • 0 is 1 (default: 2); set 3 to stream answer text into the preview instead of a status draft
  • short initial answer previews are debounced, then materialized after a bounded delay if the run is still active
  • 0 keeps one editable status draft for tool progress, shows the stable status label when answer activity arrives before tool progress, clears it at completion, and sends the final answer as a normal message
  • 0 controls whether tool/progress updates reuse the same edited preview message (default: 1 when preview streaming is active)
  • 0 controls command/exec detail inside those lines: 1 (default) or 2 (tool label only)
  • 0 (default: 1) opts into assistant commentary/preamble text in the temporary progress draft
  • legacy 0, boolean 1 values, and retired native draft preview keys are detected; run 2 to migrate them

Tool-progress lines are the short status updates shown while tools run (command execution, file reads, planning updates, patch summaries, Codex preamble/commentary in app-server mode). Telegram keeps these on by default (matches released behavior from 0+).

Keep answer-preview edits but hide tool-progress lines:

json

{ "channels": { "telegram": { "streaming": { "mode": "partial", "preview": { "toolProgress": false } } } }}

Keep tool-progress visible but hide command/exec text:

json

{ "channels": { "telegram": { "streaming": { "mode": "partial", "preview": { "commandText": "status" } } } }}

0 mode shows tool progress without editing the final answer into that message. Put the command-text policy under 1:

json

{ "channels": { "telegram": { "streaming": { "mode": "progress", "progress": { "toolProgress": true, "commandText": "status" } } } }}

0 disables preview edits and suppresses generic tool/progress chatter instead of sending it as standalone status messages; approval prompts, media, and errors still route through normal final delivery. 1 keeps only answer-preview edits.

For text-only replies: short previews get the final edit in place; long finals that split into multiple messages reuse the preview as the first chunk, then send only the remainder; progress-mode finals clear the status draft and use normal final delivery; if the final edit fails before completion is confirmed, OpenClaw falls back to normal final delivery and cleans up the stale preview. For complex replies (media payloads), OpenClaw always falls back to normal final delivery and cleans up the preview.

Preview streaming and block streaming are mutually exclusive — when block streaming is explicitly enabled, OpenClaw skips the preview stream to avoid double-streaming.

Reasoning: 0 streams reasoning into the live preview while generating, then deletes the reasoning preview after final delivery (use 1 to keep it visible). The final answer is sent without reasoning text.

Rich message formatting

Outbound text uses standard Telegram HTML messages by default, readable across current clients: bold, italic, links, code, spoilers, quotes — not Bot API 10.2 rich-only blocks (native tables, details, rich media, formulas).

Opt into Bot API 10.2 rich messages:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { richMessages: true,},},}

When enabled: the agent is told rich messages are available for this bot/account (with the supported Markdown + HTML-island authoring contract); Markdown text renders through OpenClaw’s Markdown IR as typed Bot API 10.2 rich blocks (headings, tables, details, checklists, rich media, formulas, maps, collages); media captions still use Telegram HTML captions (rich messages do not replace captions, and captions cap at 1024 characters).

This keeps model text away from Telegram’s rich-Markdown sigils, so currency like 0 is not parsed as math. Long rich text splits automatically across Telegram’s limits. Tables over the 20-column limit fall back to a code block.

Default: off, for client compatibility — some current Desktop, Web, Android, and third-party clients render accepted rich messages as unsupported. Keep this off unless every client used with the bot can render them. 0 shows whether the current session has rich messages on or off.

Link previews are on by default. 0 disables automatic entity detection for rich text.

Native commands and custom commands

Telegram’s command menu is registered at startup with 0. 1 enables native commands for Telegram.

Add custom command menu entries:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { customCommands: [ { command: "backup", description: "Git backup" }, { command: "generate", description: "Create an image" }, ],},},}

Rules: names are normalized (strip leading 0, lowercase); valid pattern 1, 2, 3, length 1-32; custom commands cannot override native commands; conflicts/duplicates are skipped and logged.

Custom commands are menu entries only — they do not auto-implement behavior. Plugin/skill commands can still work when typed even if not shown in the Telegram menu. If native commands are disabled, built-ins are removed; custom/plugin commands may still register if configured.

Common setup failures:

  • 0 with 1 after a trim retry means the menu still overflows; reduce plugin/skill/custom commands or disable 2.
  • 0, 1, or 2 failing with 3 while direct Bot API curl commands work usually means 4 was set to the full 5 endpoint. 6 must be the Bot API root only; 7 removes an accidental trailing 8.
  • 0 means Telegram rejected the configured bot token. Update 1, 2, or 3 (default account) with the current BotFather token; OpenClaw stops before polling so this is not reported as a webhook cleanup failure.
  • 0 with network/fetch errors usually means outbound DNS/HTTPS to 1 is blocked.
Device pairing commands (0 plugin)

When installed:

  1. 0 generates a setup code
  2. paste the code in the iOS app
  3. 0 lists pending requests (including role/scopes)
  4. approve: 0, 1 (only pending request), or 2

If a device retries with changed auth details (role, scopes, public key), the previous pending request is superseded with a new 0; re-run 1 before approving.

More detail: Pairing.

Inline buttons

Configure inline keyboard scope:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { capabilities: { inlineButtons: "allowlist", },},},}

Per-account override:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { accounts: { main: { capabilities: { inlineButtons: "allowlist", }, }, },},},}

Scopes: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (default). Legacy 5 maps to 6.

Message action example:

json5

{action: "send",channel: "telegram",to: "123456789",message: "Choose an option:",buttons: [[ { text: "Yes", callback_data: "yes" }, { text: "No", callback_data: "no" },],[{ text: "Cancel", callback_data: "cancel" }],],}

Mini App button example:

json5

{action: "send",channel: "telegram",to: "123456789",message: "Open app:",presentation: {blocks: [ { type: "buttons", buttons: [{ label: "Launch", web_app: { url: "https://example.com/app" } }], },],},}

0 buttons only work in private chats between a user and the bot.

Callback clicks not claimed by a registered plugin interactive handler are passed to the agent as text: 0.

Telegram message actions for agents and automation

Actions:

  • 0 (1, 2, optional 3, 4, 5)
  • 0 (1, 2, 3)
  • 0 (1, 2)
  • 0 (1, 2, 3 or 4, optional 5 inline buttons; button-only edits update reply markup)
  • 0 (1, 2, optional 3, 4)

Ergonomic aliases: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

Gating: 0, 1, 2, 3 (default: disabled). 4, 5, and 6 are enabled by default with no dedicated toggle. Runtime sends use the active config/secrets snapshot from startup/reload, so action paths do not re-resolve 7 values per send.

Reaction removal semantics: /tools/reactions.

Reply threading tags

Explicit reply threading tags in generated output:

  • 0 — replies to the triggering message
  • 0 — replies to a specific message ID

0: 1 (default), 2, 3.

When reply threading is enabled and the original text/caption is available, OpenClaw adds a native quote excerpt automatically. Telegram caps native quote text at 1024 UTF-16 code units; longer messages are quoted from the start and fall back to a plain reply if Telegram rejects the quote.

0 disables implicit reply threading only; explicit 1 tags are still honored.

Forum topics and thread behavior

Forum supergroups: topic session keys append 0; replies and typing target the topic thread; topic config path is 1.

General topic (0) is a special case: message sends omit 1 (Telegram rejects 2 with “thread not found”), but typing actions still include 3 (empirically required for the typing indicator to appear).

Topic entries inherit group settings unless overridden (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). 6 is topic-only and does not inherit from group defaults. 7 sets defaults for every topic in that group; exact topic IDs still win over 8.

Per-topic agent routing: each topic can route to a different agent via 0 in the topic config, giving it its own workspace, memory, and session:

json5

{ channels: { telegram: { groups: { "-1001234567890": { topics: { "1": { agentId: "main" }, // General topic -> main agent "3": { agentId: "zu" }, // Dev topic -> zu agent "5": { agentId: "coder" } // Code review -> coder agent } } } } }}

Each topic then has its own session key, for example 0.

Persistent ACP topic binding: forum topics can pin ACP harness sessions through top-level typed bindings (0 with 1, 2, 3, and a topic-qualified id like 4). Currently scoped to forum topics in groups/supergroups. See ACP Agents.

Thread-bound ACP spawn from chat: 0 binds the current topic to a new ACP session; follow-ups route there directly, and OpenClaw pins the spawn confirmation in-topic. Controlled by 1 (default: 2).

Template context exposes 0 and 1. DM chats with 2 keep reply metadata but only use thread-aware session keys when Telegram 3 reports 4. The retired 5 and 6 overrides are gone; BotFather threaded mode is the single source of truth. Run 7 to remove stale config keys.

Audio, video, and stickers

Audio messages

Telegram distinguishes voice notes from audio files. Default: audio-file behavior; tag 0 in the agent reply to force a voice-note send. Inbound voice-note transcripts are framed as machine-generated, untrusted text in agent context, but mention detection still uses the raw transcript so mention-gated voice messages keep working.

json5

{action: "send",channel: "telegram",to: "123456789",media: "https://example.com/voice.ogg",asVoice: true,}
Video messages

Telegram distinguishes video files from video notes. Video notes do not support captions; provided message text sends separately.

json5

{action: "send",channel: "telegram",to: "123456789",media: "https://example.com/video.mp4",asVideoNote: true,}
Locations and venues

Use the existing 0 action with one standalone 1 object. Coordinates send a native pin; adding both 2 and 3 sends a native venue card. Location sends cannot be combined with message text or media.

json5

{action: "send",channel: "telegram",to: "123456789",location: {latitude: 48.858844,longitude: 2.294351,accuracy: 12,name: "Eiffel Tower",address: "Champ de Mars, Paris",},}
Stickers

Inbound: static WEBP is downloaded and processed (placeholder 0); animated TGS and video WEBM are skipped.

Sticker context fields: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Descriptions are cached in OpenClaw SQLite plugin state to reduce repeated vision calls.

Enable sticker actions:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { actions: { sticker: true, },},},}

Send:

json5

{action: "sticker",channel: "telegram",to: "123456789",fileId: "CAACAgIAAxkBAAI...",}

Search cached stickers:

json5

{action: "sticker-search",channel: "telegram",query: "cat waving",limit: 5,}

Reaction notifications

Telegram reactions arrive as 0 updates, separate from message payloads. When enabled, OpenClaw enqueues system events like 1.

  • 0: 1 (default: 2)
  • 0: 1 (default: 2)

0 means user reactions to bot-sent messages only (best-effort via a sent-message cache). Reaction events still respect Telegram access controls (1, 2, 3, 4); unauthorized senders are dropped.

Telegram does not provide thread IDs in reaction updates: non-forum groups route to the group chat session; forum groups route to the general-topic session (0), not the exact originating topic.

0 for polling/webhook include 1 automatically.

Ack reactions

0 sends an acknowledgement emoji while OpenClaw processes an inbound message. 1 decides when it is sent.

Emoji resolution order:

  • 0
  • 0
  • 0
  • agent identity emoji fallback (0, else “👀”)

Telegram expects a unicode emoji (for example “👀”); use 0 to disable the reaction for a channel or account.

Scope (0, default 1; no Telegram-account or Telegram-channel override today):

0 (DMs + groups, including ambient room events), 1 (DMs only), 2 (every group message except ambient room events, no DMs), 3 (groups when the bot is mentioned; no DMs — default), 4 / 5 (disabled).

Config writes from Telegram events and commands

Channel config writes are enabled by default (0). Telegram-triggered writes include group migration events (1, updates 2) and 3 / 4 (requires command enablement).

Disable:

json5

{channels: {telegram: { configWrites: false,},},}

Long polling vs webhook

Default is long polling. For webhook mode, set 0 and 1; optional 2 (default 3), 4 (default 5), 6 (default 7), 8 (self-signed cert PEM for direct-IP or no-domain setups).

In long-polling mode, OpenClaw persists its restart watermark only after an update dispatches successfully; a failed handler leaves that update retryable in the same process instead of marking it completed.

The local listener binds to 0 by default. For public ingress, put a reverse proxy in front of the local port, or set 1 intentionally.

Webhook mode validates request guards, the Telegram secret token, and the JSON body, then commits the update to its durable ingress queue before returning an empty 0. Successful durable adoption includes 1; health, routing, authentication, validation, and storage-error responses omit this header. Reverse proxies and host controllers can require the header to distinguish OpenClaw adoption from a generic empty 2 without inferring acceptance from response timing.

After the durable write, OpenClaw claims and processes updates through the core channel-ingress drain (per-chat/per-topic lanes, complete at turn adoption, pre-adoption stall timeout). Slow agent turns do not hold Telegram’s delivery ACK.

Limits and CLI targets

  • 0 default 4000; 1 prefers paragraph boundaries (blank lines) before length splitting.
  • 0 (default 100) caps inbound and outbound media size.
  • group context history uses 0 or 1 (default 50); 2 disables.
  • reply/quote/forward supplemental context normalizes into one selected conversation context window when the gateway has observed the parent messages; the observed-message cache lives in OpenClaw SQLite plugin state, and 0 imports legacy sidecars. Telegram only includes one shallow 1 per update, so chains older than the cache are limited to that payload.
  • Telegram allowlists primarily gate who can trigger the agent, not a full supplemental-context redaction boundary.
  • DM history: 0, 1.

CLI and message-tool send targets accept a numeric chat ID, username, or forum topic target:

bash

openclaw message send --channel telegram --target 123456789 --message "hi"openclaw message send --channel telegram --target @name --message "hi"openclaw message send --channel telegram --target -1001234567890:topic:42 --message "hi topic"

Polls use 0 and support forum topics:

bash

openclaw message poll --channel telegram --target 123456789 \--poll-question "Ship it?" --poll-option "Yes" --poll-option "No"openclaw message poll --channel telegram --target -1001234567890:topic:42 \--poll-question "Pick a time" --poll-option "10am" --poll-option "2pm" \--poll-duration-seconds 300 --poll-public

Telegram-only poll flags: 0 (5-600), 1, 2, 3 (or a 4 target). 5 repeats 2-12 times (Telegram’s option cap).

Telegram send also supports 0 with 1 blocks for inline keyboards (when 2 allows it), 3 or 4 to request pinned delivery when the bot can pin in that chat, and 5 to send outbound images, GIFs, and videos as documents instead of compressed/animated/video uploads.

Action gating: 0 disables all outbound messages including polls; 1 disables poll creation while leaving regular sends enabled.

Exec approvals in Telegram

Telegram supports exec approvals in approver DMs and can optionally post prompts in the originating chat or topic. Approvers must be numeric Telegram user IDs.

  • 0 (1 enables when at least one approver is resolvable)
  • 0 (falls back to numeric owner IDs from 1)
  • 0: 1 (default) | 2 | 3
  • 0, 1

0, 1, and 2 control who can talk to the bot and where it sends normal replies — they do not make someone an exec approver. The first approved DM pairing bootstraps 3 when no command owner exists yet, so one-owner setups work without duplicating IDs under 4.

Channel delivery shows the command text in the chat; only enable 0 or 1 in trusted groups/topics. When the prompt lands in a forum topic, OpenClaw preserves the topic for the approval prompt and follow-up. Exec approvals expire after 30 minutes by default.

Inline approval buttons also require 0 to allow the target surface (1, 2, or 3). Approval IDs prefixed with 4 resolve through plugin approvals; others resolve through exec approvals first.

See Exec approvals.

Error reply controls

When the agent hits a delivery or provider error, the error policy controls whether error messages reach the Telegram chat:

  • channels.telegram.errorPolicy
  • Values: always , once , silent
  • Default: always
  • Description: always sends every error message to the chat. once sends each unique error message once per built-in cooldown window. silent never sends error messages to the chat.

Per-account, per-group, and per-topic overrides are supported (same inheritance as other Telegram config keys).

json5

{ channels: { telegram: { errorPolicy: "always", groups: { "-1001234567890": { errorPolicy: "silent", // suppress errors in this group }, }, }, },}

Troubleshooting

Bot does not respond to non mention group messages

  • If 0, Telegram privacy mode must allow full visibility: BotFather 1 -> Disable, then remove + re-add the bot to the group.
  • 0 warns when config expects unmentioned group messages.
  • 0 checks explicit numeric group IDs; wildcard 1 cannot be membership-probed.
  • Quick session test: 0.

Bot not seeing group messages at all

  • When 0 exists, the group must be listed (or include 1).
  • Verify bot membership in the group.
  • Review 0 for skip reasons.

Commands work partially or not at all

  • Authorize your sender identity (pairing and/or numeric 0); command authorization still applies even when group policy is 1.
  • 0 with 1 means the native menu has too many entries; reduce plugin/skill/custom commands or disable native menus.
  • 0 / 1 startup calls and 2 typing calls are bounded and retry once through Telegram’s transport fallback on request timeout. Persistent network/fetch errors usually mean DNS/HTTPS to 3 is unreachable.

Startup reports unauthorized token

  • 0 is a Telegram auth failure for the configured bot token. Re-copy or regenerate the token in BotFather, then update 1, 2, 3, or 4 (default account).
  • 0 during startup is also an auth failure; treating it as “no webhook exists” would only defer the same bad-token failure to a later API call.

Polling or network instability

  • Node 22+ with a custom fetch/proxy can trigger immediate abort behavior if 0 types mismatch.
  • Some hosts resolve 0 to IPv6 first; broken IPv6 egress causes intermittent API failures.
  • Logs with 0 or 1 are retried as recoverable network errors.
  • During polling startup, OpenClaw reuses the successful startup 0 probe for grammY so the runner does not need a second 1 before the first 2.
  • If 0 fails with a transient network error during polling startup, OpenClaw continues into long polling instead of making another pre-poll control-plane call. A still-active webhook then surfaces as a 1 conflict; OpenClaw rebuilds the transport and retries webhook cleanup.
  • 0 in logs means OpenClaw restarts polling and rebuilds the transport after 120 seconds without completed long-poll liveness by default.
  • 0 and 1 warn when a running polling account has not completed 2 after startup grace, a running webhook account has not completed 3 after startup grace, or the last successful polling transport activity is stale.
  • Telegram honors process proxy env for Bot API transport: 0, 1, 2, and lowercase variants. 3 / 4 can still bypass 5.
  • If 0 is set for a service environment and no standard proxy env is present, Telegram uses that URL for Bot API transport too.
  • On VPS hosts with unstable direct egress/TLS, route Telegram API calls through a proxy:

yaml

channels:telegram:proxy: socks5://<user>:<password>@proxy-host:1080
  • Node 22+ defaults to 0 (except WSL2). Telegram DNS result order honors 1, then 2, then the process default (for example 3), falling back to 4 on Node 22+ if none applies.
  • On WSL2, or when IPv4-only behavior works better, force family selection:

yaml

channels:telegram:network: autoSelectFamily: false
  • RFC 2544 benchmark-range answers (0) are already allowed for Telegram media downloads by default. If a trusted fake-IP or transparent proxy rewrites 1 to some other private/internal/special-use address during media downloads, opt in to the Telegram-only bypass:

yaml

channels:telegram:network: dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true

  • The same opt-in is available per account at 0.

  • If your proxy resolves Telegram media hosts into 0, leave the dangerous flag off first — that range is already allowed by default.

  • Temporary environment overrides: 0, 1, 2.

  • Validate DNS answers:

bash

dig +short api.telegram.org Adig +short api.telegram.org AAAA

More help: Channel troubleshooting.

Tlon

ChannelsDeveloper and self-hosted

Tlon is a decentralized messenger built on Urbit. OpenClaw connects to your Urbit ship and responds to DMs and group chat messages. Group replies require an @ mention by default, with authorization rules and an owner-approval flow layered on top.

Status: bundled plugin. DMs, group mentions, threads, rich text, image upload/download, and an owner approval system are supported. Reactions and polls are not.

Bundled plugin

Tlon ships bundled in current OpenClaw releases; packaged builds do not need a separate install.

On an older build or custom install that excludes it, install from npm:

bash

openclaw plugins install @openclaw/tlon

Use the bare package name to track the current release tag. Pin a version (0) only for reproducible installs.

From a local checkout:

bash

openclaw plugins install ./path/to/local/tlon-plugin

Details: Plugins

Setup

bash

openclaw channels add --channel tlon --ship ~sampel-palnet --url https://your-ship-host --code lidlut-tabwed-pillex-ridrup

Or edit config directly:

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { enabled: true, ship: "~sampel-palnet", url: "https://your-ship-host", code: "lidlut-tabwed-pillex-ridrup", ownerShip: "~your-main-ship", // recommended: your ship, always authorized }, },}

Restart the gateway after editing config directly. Then DM the bot or @ mention it in a group channel.

Inbound durability

OpenClaw persists accepted Tlon DM and group-chat events before agent dispatch. Pending or retryable turns survive a Gateway restart, and work remains serialized per group channel or direct peer. Stable Urbit message IDs also suppress a redelivered event while its queue record or retained completion record exists.

Delivery is at least once across the queue-to-agent boundary: a crash during handoff can replay a turn. Agent actions that produce external side effects should therefore remain idempotent where practical.

Private/LAN ships

OpenClaw blocks private/internal hostnames and IP ranges for SSRF protection by default. If your ship runs on a private network (localhost, LAN IP, internal hostname), opt in explicitly:

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { url: "http://localhost:8080", network: { dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true, }, }, },}

Applies to targets like 0, 1, and 2. Only enable this for a ship URL you trust; it disables SSRF protection for that account’s HTTP requests.

Group channels

Pin channels manually, or turn on auto-discovery:

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { groupChannels: ["chat/~host-ship/general", "chat/~host-ship/support"], autoDiscoverChannels: true, }, },}

0 defaults to 1 when unset in config; the setup wizard defaults the prompt to yes and writes 2 explicitly. With it on, OpenClaw scries joined groups on startup, watches new channels as group invites are accepted, and rechecks every 2 minutes.

Access control

DM allowlist (empty = no DMs allowed unless the sender is 0):

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { dmAllowlist: ["~zod", "~nec"], }, },}

Group authorization defaults to 0 per channel. Set 1 for a baseline, and override per channel nest:

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { defaultAuthorizedShips: ["~zod"], authorization: { channelRules: { "chat/~host-ship/general": { mode: "restricted", allowedShips: ["~zod", "~nec"], }, "chat/~host-ship/announcements": { mode: "open", }, }, }, }, },}

Once the bot has replied inside a thread, it keeps responding to later messages in that thread without requiring another mention.

Set 0 to require a new explicit mention for those follow-ups. Account overrides use 1. Tlon does not currently produce 2 or 3 facts, so those flags have no effect here.

Owner and approval system

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { ownerShip: "~your-main-ship", }, },}

The owner ship is authorized everywhere: DM invites are always auto-accepted, group invites are always auto-accepted, and channel messages always pass authorization. The owner does not need to be in 0, 1, or 2.

When 0 is set, unauthorized requests do not just get dropped — they queue a pending approval and DM the owner:

  • DM requests from ships not on 0
  • Mentions in channels where the sender fails authorization
  • Group invites from ships not on 0 (when auto-accept is off, or on but the inviter is not allowlisted)

The owner replies in DM to act on a request:

  • approve / deny / block
  • Effect: Acts on the most recent pending approval
  • approve / deny
  • Effect: Acts on a specific approval by id
  • block
  • Effect: Also blocks the ship natively so it cannot reconnect
  • unblock ~ship
  • Effect: Reverses a native block
  • blocked
  • Effect: Lists currently blocked ships
  • pending
  • Effect: Lists pending approval requests

Without 0 configured, unauthorized DMs and channel mentions are just dropped and logged; there is no approval prompt.

Auto-accept settings

Auto-accept DM invites from ships already on 0 (the owner is always auto-accepted regardless of this flag):

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { autoAcceptDmInvites: true, }, },}

Auto-accept group invites from an allowlist (fails closed: with 0 and an empty 1, no non-owner invite is accepted):

json5

{ channels: { tlon: { autoAcceptGroupInvites: true, groupInviteAllowlist: ["~zod"], }, },}

Hot-reload via Urbit settings store

Most of the settings above (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) are mirrored into the ship’s 9 agent (desk 10, bucket 11) on first run and then read live from there, so changes made via a Landscape client or the bundled skill’s settings commands apply without a gateway restart. 12 and pending approvals are also persisted there as JSON. File config stays the source of truth for values never written to the settings store.

Delivery targets (CLI/cron)

Use with 0 or cron delivery:

  • DM: 0 or 1
  • Group: 0 or 1

Bundled skill

The plugin bundles 0, a CLI for direct Urbit operations, available automatically once the plugin is installed:

  • Activity: mentions, replies, unreads
  • Channels: list, create, rename
  • Contacts: list/get/update profiles
  • Groups: create, join, invite/request flows, roles
  • Hooks: manage channel hooks
  • Messages: history, search
  • DMs: send, react, accept/decline
  • Posts: react, delete
  • Notebook: post to diary channels
  • Settings: hot-reload plugin config via the settings store above

Capabilities

  • Direct messages
  • Status: Supported
  • Groups/channels
  • Status: Supported (mention-gated by default)
  • Threads
  • Status: Supported (keeps replying once it has joined)
  • Rich text
  • Status: Markdown converted to Tlon’s native format
  • Images
  • Status: Downloaded inbound, uploaded outbound
  • Reactions
  • Status: Only via the bundled skill
  • Polls
  • Status: Not supported
  • Native commands
  • Status: Owner-only by default

Troubleshooting

bash

openclaw statusopenclaw gateway statusopenclaw logs --followopenclaw doctor

Common failures:

  • DMs ignored: sender not in 0 and no 1 configured for the approval flow.
  • Group messages ignored: channel not discovered/pinned, or sender fails authorization with no 0 to queue an approval.
  • Connection errors: check the ship URL is reachable; set 0 for local ships.
  • Auth errors: login codes rotate — copy the current code from your ship.

Configuration reference

Full configuration: Configuration

  • channels.tlon.enabled
  • Meaning: Enable/disable channel startup.
  • channels.tlon.ship
  • Meaning: Bot’s Urbit ship name (e.g. ~sampel-palnet ).
  • channels.tlon.url
  • Meaning: Ship URL (e.g. 0 ).
  • channels.tlon.code
  • Meaning: Ship login code.
  • channels.tlon.network.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork
  • Meaning: Allow localhost/LAN ship URLs (SSRF opt-in).
  • channels.tlon.ownerShip
  • Meaning: Owner ship: always authorized, receives approval requests.
  • channels.tlon.dmAllowlist
  • Meaning: Ships allowed to DM (empty = none besides owner).
  • channels.tlon.autoAcceptDmInvites
  • Meaning: Auto-accept DMs from ships in dmAllowlist .
  • channels.tlon.autoAcceptGroupInvites
  • Meaning: Auto-accept group invites from groupInviteAllowlist .
  • channels.tlon.groupInviteAllowlist
  • Meaning: Ships whose group invites are auto-accepted.
  • channels.tlon.autoDiscoverChannels
  • Meaning: Auto-discover joined group channels (default: false ).
  • channels.tlon.implicitMentions.threadParticipation
  • Meaning: Let participated-thread follow-ups bypass mention gating.
  • channels.tlon.groupChannels
  • Meaning: Manually pinned channel nests.
  • channels.tlon.defaultAuthorizedShips
  • Meaning: Ships authorized for all channels (used when no rule matches).
  • channels.tlon.authorization.channelRules
  • Meaning: Per-channel-nest auth mode + allowlist.
  • channels.tlon.showModelSignature
  • Meaning: Append _[Generated by ]_ to replies.
  • channels.tlon.responsePrefix
  • Meaning: Static prefix prepended to outbound replies.
  • channels.tlon.accounts.
  • Meaning: Additional named accounts (multi-ship setups).

Notes

  • Group replies need an @ mention (e.g. 0) unless the bot already joined that thread.
  • Thread replies land in-thread; the bot also gets the last 10 messages of thread context prepended for the agent.
  • Rich text (bold, italic, code, headers, lists) converts to Tlon’s native format.
  • Sending an inbound message that asks for a channel summary (for example “summarize this channel”) triggers a built-in history summarization instead of the normal reply flow.

Twitch

ChannelsDeveloper and self-hosted

Twitch chat support over Twitch’s chat (IRC) interface via the Twurple client. OpenClaw signs in as a Twitch bot account, joins one channel per configured account, and replies in that channel.

Install

Twitch ships as an official plugin; it is not part of the core install.

npm registry

bash

openclaw plugins install @openclaw/twitch
Local checkout

bash

openclaw plugins install ./path/to/local/twitch-plugin

0 registers and enables the plugin. Picking Twitch during 1 or 2 installs it on demand. Use the bare package name to follow the current release; pin an exact version only for reproducible installs. Requires OpenClaw 2026.4.10 or newer.

Details: Plugins

Quick setup

Install the plugin

See Install above.

Create a Twitch bot account

Create a dedicated Twitch account for the bot (or use an existing account).

Generate credentials

Use Twitch Token Generator:

  • Select Bot Token
  • Verify scopes 0 and 1 are selected
  • Copy the Client ID and Access Token
Find your Twitch user ID

Use convert twitch username to user id to convert a username to a Twitch user ID.

Configure the token
  • Env: 0 (default account only)
  • Or config: 0

If both are set, config takes precedence (the env var is only a fallback for the default account).

Start the gateway

bash

openclaw gateway run

Minimal config:

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { enabled: true, username: "openclaw", // Bot's Twitch account (authenticates) accessToken: "oauth:abc123...", // OAuth access token (or use OPENCLAW_TWITCH_ACCESS_TOKEN env var) clientId: "xyz789...", // Client ID from Token Generator channel: "yourchannel", // Which Twitch channel's chat to join (required) allowFrom: ["123456789"], // (recommended) Your Twitch user ID only }, },}

What it is

  • A Twitch channel owned by the Gateway.
  • Deterministic routing: replies always go back to the Twitch channel the message came from.
  • Each joined channel maps to an isolated group session key 0.
  • 0 is the bot’s account (who authenticates), 1 is which chat room to join. One account entry joins exactly one channel.
  • Tokens work with or without the 0 prefix; OpenClaw normalizes both ways (the setup wizard expects the 1 form).

Inbound durability

OpenClaw durably queues each accepted Twitch chat message before normal dispatch. Pending or retryable messages survive a Gateway restart, stay serialized for the configured channel, and use Twitch’s message ID to suppress duplicate queue entries while the active or retained completion record exists.

Twitch chat does not replay a 0 after the client has accepted it. This protects the local accept-to-dispatch crash window, but it cannot recover messages missed before durable admission. If the queue append itself fails, OpenClaw logs the failure; reconnecting does not ask Twitch to resend that message.

Token refresh (optional)

Tokens from Twitch Token Generator cannot be refreshed by OpenClaw - regenerate when expired (they last a few hours; no app registration needed).

For automatic refresh, create your own app at the Twitch Developer Console and add:

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { clientSecret: "your_client_secret", refreshToken: "your_refresh_token", }, },}

With both set, the plugin uses a refreshing auth provider that renews tokens before expiration and logs each refresh. Without 0 it logs 1; without 2 it falls back to a static (non-refreshing) token.

Multi-account support

Use 0 with per-account credentials. See Configuration for the shared pattern.

Example (one bot account in two channels):

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { accounts: { channel1: { username: "openclaw", accessToken: "oauth:abc123...", clientId: "xyz789...", channel: "yourchannel", }, channel2: { username: "openclaw", accessToken: "oauth:def456...", clientId: "uvw012...", channel: "secondchannel", }, }, }, },}

Access control

0 is a hard allowlist of Twitch user IDs. When it is set, 1 is ignored; leave 2 unset to use role-based access instead.

Available roles: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

User ID allowlist (most secure)

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { accounts: { default: { allowFrom: ["123456789", "987654321"], }, }, }, },}
Role-based

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { accounts: { default: { allowedRoles: ["moderator", "vip"], }, }, }, },}
Disable @mention requirement

By default, 0 is 1. To respond to all allowed messages:

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { accounts: { default: { requireMention: false, }, }, }, },}

Troubleshooting

First, run diagnostic commands:

bash

openclaw doctoropenclaw channels status --probe

Bot does not respond to messages

  • Check access control: Ensure your user ID is in 0, or temporarily remove 1 and set 2 to test.
  • Check the mention gate: With 0 (default), messages must @mention the bot username.
  • Check the bot is in the channel: The bot only joins the channel named in 0.

Token issues

“Failed to connect” or authentication errors:

  • Verify 0 is the OAuth access token value (the 1 prefix is optional)
  • Check the token has 0 and 1 scopes
  • If using token refresh, verify 0 and 1 are set

Token refresh not working

Check logs for refresh events:

text

Using env token source for mybotAccess token refreshed for user 123456 (expires in 14400s)

If you see 0:

  • Ensure 0 is provided
  • Ensure 0 is provided

Config

Account config

Bot username (the authenticating account).

OAuth access token with 0 and 1 (config or env for the default account).

Twitch Client ID (from Token Generator or your app). Optional in the schema but required to connect.

Channel to join.

Enable this account.

Optional: for automatic token refresh.

Optional: for automatic token refresh.

Token expiry in seconds (refresh tracking).

Timestamp when the token was obtained (refresh tracking).

User ID allowlist. When set, roles are ignored.

Require @mention to trigger the bot.

Outbound response prefix override for this account.

Provider options
  • 0 - Enable/disable channel startup
  • 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 - Simplified single-account config (implicit 4 account; takes precedence over 5)
  • 0 - Multi-account config (all account fields above)
  • 0 - Which account name is the default
  • 0 - Markdown table rendering mode (1 | 2 | 3 | 4)

Full example:

json5

{ channels: { twitch: { enabled: true, username: "openclaw", accessToken: "oauth:abc123...", clientId: "xyz789...", channel: "yourchannel", clientSecret: "secret123...", refreshToken: "refresh456...", allowFrom: ["123456789"], accounts: { second: { username: "mybot", accessToken: "oauth:def456...", clientId: "uvw012...", channel: "your_channel", enabled: true, expiresIn: 14400, obtainmentTimestamp: 1706092800000, allowedRoles: ["moderator"], }, }, }, },}

Tool actions

The agent can send Twitch messages through the message tool 0 action:

json5

{ channel: "twitch", action: "send", to: "#mychannel", message: "Hello Twitch!",}

0 is optional and defaults to the account’s configured 1.

Safety and ops

  • Treat tokens like passwords - never commit tokens to git.
  • Use automatic token refresh for long-running bots.
  • Use user ID allowlists instead of usernames for access control.
  • Monitor logs for token refresh events and connection status.
  • Scope tokens minimally - only request 0 and 1.
  • If stuck: restart the gateway after confirming no other process owns the session.

Limits

  • 500 characters per message; longer replies are chunked at word boundaries.
  • Markdown is stripped before sending (Twitch chat is plain text; newlines become spaces).
  • OpenClaw adds no rate limiting of its own; the Twurple chat client handles Twitch rate limits.
